### 3.1.1 Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions: From Goffman’s Sociology to Algorithmic Behavioral Engineering

Within the landscape of contemporary cyber-psychological discourse, the intersection between large language models and human cognitive architectures has birthed an unprecedented epistemological battleground. The genealogy of framing theory—rooted in the micro-sociology of Erving Goffman (1974) and radically radicalized within behavioral economics by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky (1979; 1984)—is undergoing a staggering metamorphosis. Whereas framing was once understood as a conventional rhetorical strategy employed by politicians, journalists, or advertisers to highlight specific aspects of a reality while muting others, today, under the command of generative algorithms, framing has mutated into an autonomous, adaptive, and covert instrument of behavioral engineering.

The epistemology of this phenomenon demands that we dismantle the classical assumptions regarding human rationality that have been celebrated by orthodox economic schools
